701.title: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
701.hook: Garuda steals the nectar of the gods to buy his mother's freedom, and never tastes a drop
701.carry: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
701.tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
701.howItsDone: In some Vishnu temples Garuda stands facing the shrine with folded hands, as Vishnu's mount, and kusha grass is used in some Hindu rites. Some families retell Garuda's story to children as a story of loyalty to a mother.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Adi Parva: Kadru's bet, black hairs on a white horse, and a curse on the sons who refused to cheat. Did someone ask you to tip the scales? Day seven hundred one.

An egg cracks open and something blazing comes out, so bright the gods take it for fire. It's Garuda, Vinata's son, a bird of enormous strength. He grows up to find his mother a slave to her sister, made to carry the snakes wherever they want to go. So he asks the snakes the obvious question: what would it take to set her free? They name a price nobody could pay. Bring us the amrita, the nectar of immortality, which the gods keep for themselves.
screen: `A BLAZING EGG.` → `HIS MOTHER, A SLAVE.` → `THE PRICE: THE GODS' NECTAR.`

segments.voice: So Garuda goes to get it. The Adi Parva makes it a full adventure: he fights the gods who guard it, slips past a spinning wheel of blades, and gets by the fierce guardians beside the nectar. He takes the amrita. And here's the first surprise. He doesn't drink it. He could make himself immortal on the spot, and he carries it away untouched, because it's for his mother's freedom. Vishnu sees this and is so pleased that he grants Garuda boons: a place on Vishnu's banner, and immortality without a drop of the nectar. Garuda offers a boon in return, and Vishnu asks him to be his mount, the great bird he rides. Indra, king of the gods, strikes him with the thunderbolt, and Garuda, the text says, lets a single feather fall out of respect for it, and nothing more. Then Indra asks for the nectar back. Garuda makes him an offer: I've promised it to the snakes, and I'll let no one drink it. But wherever I set it down, you may take it up. They part as friends. Then the second surprise. Garuda brings the nectar to the snakes, sets it down on a bed of kusha grass, and says: here it is. My mother is free. Go and bathe before you drink. The snakes agree, and Vinata is free. While the snakes are bathing, Indra comes down, just as they agreed, and takes the amrita back to heaven. The snakes come back to an empty bed of grass, and they lick it, hoping for a drop. The sharp grass splits their tongues. That, the story says, is why snakes have forked tongues, and why kusha grass is held holy: the nectar of the gods once lay on it. Garuda kept every promise to the letter. He paid the price. He freed his mother. And the snakes who held her as a slave get exactly what they bargained for, and nothing more.
screen: `HE NEVER DRINKS IT.` · `VISHNU'S MOUNT AND BANNER.` · `SET DOWN ON KUSHA GRASS.` · `INDRA TAKES IT BACK.` · then, large: `THE PRICE PAID, TO THE LETTER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Garuda carried the gods' own nectar and didn't take a sip. Bring to mind something you're carrying for someone else: an errand, a secret, a responsibility, someone's trust. Feel its weight, lightly. Breathe in, and hold it carefully. Breathe out, and notice any pull to keep a little for yourself, if there is one. Just notice. Then come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Adi Parva. The opening book, where Garuda steals the gods' nectar to free his mother, and never tastes it.

702.title: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
702.hook: a tired king drapes a dead snake on a silent sage, and a chain of small choices ends in Takshaka's bite
702.carry: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
702.tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
702.howItsDone: Vows of silence, mauna, are kept by some Hindu ascetics and by some householders for a day or a season. Parikshit's death is also the setting of the Bhagavata Purana, which tradition says was recited to him in his last days.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Adi Parva: Garuda, the nectar he never tasted, and his mother set free. What did you carry for someone else? Day seven hundred two.

A king is out hunting, and he's lost a deer he wounded. He comes on an old sage sitting very still, and asks: did a deer pass this way? The sage says nothing. He's keeping a vow of silence. The king asks again. Nothing. And the king, tired, hungry and stung, lifts a dead snake on the end of his bow and drapes it over the old man's shoulders. Then he rides home. The king is Parikshit, Janamejaya's father. The sage is Shamika. This is how Janamejaya's wound was made.
screen: `A LOST DEER, A SILENT SAGE.` → `A DEAD SNAKE ON HIS SHOULDERS.` → `JANAMEJAYA'S WOUND.`

segments.voice: Shamika doesn't move. He bears it. But his son Shringin, a young man with a hot temper and real power from his austerities, hears about it from a friend. And he curses the king: within seven nights, Takshaka, king of the snakes, will bite him, and he will die. Now watch the father. Shamika is not pleased. He tells his son that forgiveness is a sage's strength, that the king protects people like them, and he sends a disciple to warn Parikshit. The king takes the warning seriously. He builds a palace on a single pillar and fills it with guards, physicians, and holy men with mantras against poison. A sage named Kashyapa, who can cure snakebite, sets out to save the king. Takshaka meets him on the road. To test him, Takshaka bites a great tree and burns it to ash, and Kashyapa brings it back to life. So Takshaka offers him wealth to go home, and Kashyapa takes it and turns back. Then the snakes come in disguise, as ascetics carrying fruit for the king. In one fruit is a tiny insect. As the sun goes down on the seventh day, Parikshit, thinking the danger has passed, picks it up and says, half in jest: let this one bite me. The insect becomes Takshaka, coils around the king, and kills him. Look at the chain. A wounded deer. A sage's silence. A king's insult. A son's curse. A healer paid off. A joke at sunset. No single link is the whole story. That's the frame Janamejaya stands in, and his fire is the next link.
screen: `A SON'S CURSE: SEVEN NIGHTS.` · `THE FATHER SENDS A WARNING.` · `A HEALER PAID TO TURN BACK.` · `TAKSHAKA HIDDEN IN A FRUIT.` · then, large: `NO SINGLE LINK IS THE WHOLE STORY.`

segments.voice: Let the shoulders drop and the breath slow. Bring to mind a small thing you did out of tiredness or hurry: a sharp word, a door shut too hard. Follow it one link forward. What did it set going? Then let it rest. Now look for a link you could still change, today, if there is one. Don't solve it yet. Just know where it is. Breathe in on the chain. Breathe out on the one link. The bell holds the time.
Adi Parva. The opening book, where a king's careless insult and a son's curse end in Takshaka's bite.

703.title: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
703.hook: a young sage, half from the snakes' own family, asks the king for one gift: stop the fire
703.carry: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
703.howItsDone: In some Hindu households Astika's name is remembered as a protection against snakes, in keeping with the promise the story records. A reciter working through the Adi Parva in order finishes the Astika section before turning to the Kuru story proper.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Adi Parva: a dead snake on a silent sage, a son's curse, and Takshaka hidden in a fruit. Did you let someone's silence be? Day seven hundred three.
screen: `NO SINGLE LINK IS THE WHOLE STORY.`

segments.voice: The fire is lit. Janamejaya has heard how his father died, and his priests begin the snake sacrifice. As they chant, snakes are drawn from everywhere into the flames, the text says, great and small, crying out as they fall. Takshaka, the one the king most wants, has fled to Indra for protection. And a young man is walking toward the sacrifice, sent by his mother. His name is Astika. His father is a sage, his mother is the sister of a snake king, and he has come to stop the fire.
screen: `THE FIRE IS LIT.` → `TAKSHAKA HIDES WITH INDRA.` → `A YOUNG SAGE IS COMING.`

segments.voice: Astika's story starts with his father, a sage named Jaratkaru, who wanted no wife and no home. One day he found his ancestors hanging head down over a pit, holding on to a thin root that a rat was gnawing. They were falling, they told him, because their line would end with him. So Jaratkaru agreed to marry, on strange terms: only a bride who shared his name. And the snake king Vasuki had a sister named Jaratkaru. Vasuki knew his mother Kadru's curse, and he had been told that a child of this marriage would save the snakes. That child is Astika. At the sacrifice, Astika doesn't argue or threaten. He praises the king, the priests and the fire, so well that Janamejaya wants to give him a gift. Ask for anything, the king says. And Astika asks: stop the sacrifice. Janamejaya tries to bargain, offering other gifts instead. Astika says no; this is what I want. By now Indra has let go of Takshaka, and the snake king is falling toward the flames, held in the air above them. The assembly urges the king to keep his word. And Janamejaya does. The fire stops. Takshaka is spared. The text adds that the snakes, in gratitude, promised safety to those who remember Astika's story. And the text says that at this same sacrifice, Vaishampayana told Janamejaya the story of his ancestors, the Kurus and the Pandavas. So the frame closes on a king who let go of his revenge, and sat down to hear about his family's great war. On the first day of this year we met him beside a fire. We leave him listening.
screen: `A SAGE WHO WANTED NO WIFE.` · `A BRIDE WHO SHARED HIS NAME.` · `PRAISE, THEN ONE REQUEST.` · `THE KING KEEPS HIS WORD.` · then, large: `WE LEAVE HIM LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Find a steady seat and let the breathing slow. Astika stopped a fire not by fighting it, but by asking. Bring to mind something you'd like to see stop: a quarrel, a habit, a cold silence between two people. Notice whether you've been arguing with it. Then let a question form instead: what would I ask for, if someone offered? Hold it without forcing an answer. The bell holds the time.
Adi Parva. The opening book, where Astika's request ends the snake sacrifice, and the great story begins.

704.title: Shantanu and Ganga
704.hook: a king in heaven stares too long at the river goddess, and gods under a curse ask her for a terrible favor
704.howItsDone: At the Ganga, the river is honored as a goddess: pilgrims bathe in her waters, some carry Ganga water home in sealed vessels, and lamps are offered to her at evening aarti on her banks.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Adi Parva's frame closed: Astika asked, Janamejaya stopped his fire and sat down to hear the story. Did you ask plainly for what you wanted? Day seven hundred four.

A court in heaven. The gods are gathered before Brahma, and among them is a king, Mahabhisha, who earned his place there by his deeds on earth. Then the river goddess Ganga arrives. A wind lifts her garment. The gods lower their eyes. Mahabhisha doesn't. He looks, and keeps looking. Brahma sees it, and tells him: you will be born again among mortals. This part of the Kuru story starts with a stare.
screen: `A COURT IN HEAVEN.` → `THE GODS LOWER THEIR EYES.` → `ONE KING KEEPS LOOKING.`

segments.voice: This is the first piece of a new story inside the Adi Parva: Shantanu and Ganga. And the text sets it up with two curses, side by side. The first is Mahabhisha's. Brahma sends him down to be born on earth, and tells him that Ganga, the one who stole his mind, will cross him there, and that his time on earth will end when he finally loses his temper with her. Mahabhisha chooses to be born as the son of a good king named Pratipa. The second curse belongs to the Vasus, a group of gods. On her way back, Ganga meets them, downcast. The sage Vasishtha, they tell her, has cursed them to be born as men. They don't want to linger in human lives. So they ask Ganga a strange favor: be our mother on earth, and as each of us is born, throw us into your waters, so we're set free at once. Ganga agrees, with one condition: one son has to live, so that her time with the king isn't fruitless. The Vasus accept. Each of them gives a portion of his own power to that one son, who will live a long life on earth, and, they say, will have no children. Hold that last detail; it matters for a long time. Now go back to the fault that started it. Not a crime, not a lie: a look that wouldn't lower, in a hall where every other eye looked down. And Brahma's sentence is shaped to fit it. The one who took his mind in heaven will be the one who tries it on earth. Where Mahabhisha's attention went, his whole next life followed. And Ganga here is both the sacred river and a woman with a promise to keep.
screen: `MAHABHISHA: BORN AGAIN ON EARTH.` · `THE VASUS: CURSED BY VASISHTHA.` · `THROW US INTO YOUR WATERS.` · `ONE SON MUST LIVE.` · then, large: `WHERE THE EYES GO, A LIFE FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: A river keeps moving; it doesn't hold on. Let the breath do the same for a few rounds. Then let your eyes lower, or close, and notice where your attention wants to go: a screen, a worry, a face, a plan. Don't fight it. Just notice what keeps pulling your gaze back up. Each time you notice, let your attention come down to the breath again, the way the gods in Brahma's court lowered their eyes. The bell holds the time.
Shantanu and Ganga. A king born from a stare in heaven, and a river goddess who has made a promise.

705.title: Shantanu and Ganga
705.hook: a woman rises from the river and sits on a praying king's right thigh; years later his son makes her a promise
705.howItsDone: In some Hindu weddings, the couple's promises to each other are made aloud before a sacred fire.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shantanu and Ganga began with a stare in Brahma's court and the Vasus' strange bargain. What kept pulling your eyes back? Day seven hundred five.
screen: `WHERE THE EYES GO, A LIFE FOLLOWS.`

segments.voice: A king is sitting by the river, deep in prayer. His name is Pratipa. Out of the water rises a woman of great beauty, and she sits down on his right thigh. Pratipa doesn't send her away, and he doesn't take her as a lover. Instead he tells her: the right thigh is for children and daughters-in-law. The left is for a wife. You sat on the right, so you'll be my son's wife.
screen: `A WOMAN RISES FROM THE RIVER.` → `SHE SITS ON THE RIGHT THIGH.` → `YOU'LL BE MY SON'S WIFE.`

segments.voice: The woman is Ganga, and she agrees: she'll marry Pratipa's son, on one condition, that whatever she does, he won't question it. Pratipa and his queen long for a son, and a son is born: Shantanu, who is Mahabhisha come down from heaven. When Shantanu is grown, Pratipa hands the kingdom to him, and a message with it. A lovely woman may come to you, he says. If she does, take her as your wife. Don't ask who she is, and don't question what she does. Shantanu loves to hunt. One day, walking along the bank of the Ganga, he sees a woman by the water, and he's struck. He asks her to be his wife. She answers with terms. I'll be your wife, she says, but whatever I do, good or bad, you must never stop me or speak harshly to me. The moment you do, I'll leave. He agrees. Now notice what we know that Shantanu doesn't. We know she's Ganga. We know about the Vasus. We know her promise. He knows only that he's in love, and that he's given his word. Here the poem sets a promise in place long before anyone sees what it will cost. A vow made happily, in the first rush of love, becomes the thing that will hold his tongue. And notice how the old king prepared the ground. Pratipa's message reads almost like a warning, passed from father to son: when something wonderful comes, don't ask too much. They marry, and the text says they're happy together. And their first child is on the way.
screen: `SHANTANU: MAHABHISHA REBORN.` · `A FATHER'S MESSAGE: DON'T ASK.` · `HER TERMS: NEVER STOP ME.` · `WE KNOW WHAT HE DOESN'T.` · then, large: `A VOW MADE IN LOVE.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath slow. Bring to mind a promise you made easily, before you knew what it would ask of you: a job, a friendship, a commitment, a yes. Don't judge it. Just hold it. Breathe in, and remember the day you said yes. Breathe out, and notice what it has asked of you since. Keep breathing with it. The bell holds the time.
Shantanu and Ganga. A king who promises never to question his wife, and a goddess who has her reasons.

706.title: Shantanu and Ganga
706.hook: seven sons are given to the river while a king keeps his vow of silence; at the eighth, he speaks
706.howItsDone: Many Hindu families carry the ashes of their dead to the Ganga, at places such as Haridwar and Varanasi, trusting the river as Ganga is trusted in this story: as a mother whose waters release.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shantanu and Ganga by the river, and his vow never to stop or question her. Did you read the terms before you said yes? Day seven hundred six.

A son is born to the king and queen. And the queen carries the baby down to the river, and gives him to the Ganga's waters. As she does it, she says it's for his good. Shantanu watches from the bank, and says nothing. He remembers what he promised: never stop her, never speak harshly to her, or she leaves. Another son is born, and the same thing happens. And another. The text tells it plainly, without looking away.
screen: `A SON IS BORN.` → `GIVEN TO THE RIVER.` → `THE KING SAYS NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Seven sons, the text says, one after another, into the river. And Shantanu, every time, stays silent, because he's afraid that if he speaks, she'll leave him. Then the eighth son is born. As she carries this one toward the river, Shantanu can't hold it in. He speaks. Don't kill him, he says. Who are you? Why do you kill your own sons? She stops. I won't kill this one, she says. But my time with you is over, as we agreed. And she tells him who she is: Ganga, the daughter of Jahnu, the text says. The sons, she explains, were the Vasus, cursed to be born as men, and she has freed them as she promised. Now hear it from where we stand. Two days ago we heard the Vasus beg for this. Yesterday we watched the vow get made. Today we see what it cost, and the scene can be seen three ways. For Shantanu, these were his children, lost in front of him. For the Vasus, it was the release they asked for. For Ganga, it was a promise kept to the letter. The Mahabharata doesn't smooth this over. It lets the scene stay hard. Some readers take it as a story about curses and karma working themselves out. Some hear it as a picture of what an unquestioning vow can cost. Some take from it that what's seen from the riverbank isn't the whole story. And the son who lives carries the Vasus' power, and their word that he'll have no children. Ganga takes the child with her, and goes.
screen: `SEVEN SONS, AND SILENCE.` · `AT THE EIGHTH, HE SPEAKS.` · `I AM GANGA, DAUGHTER OF JAHNU.` · `THREE VIEWS OF ONE SCENE.` · then, large: `THE RIVERBANK ISN'T THE WHOLE STORY.`

segments.voice: This is a hard story, so go gently. Let the breath settle. Bring to mind something you once watched happen and didn't understand, something that looked only like loss. You don't have to find a hidden meaning in it. Some things stay hard. Just let it be seen, and breathe beside it. If there's a part you now see differently, notice that too. The bell holds the time.

707.title: Shantanu and Ganga
707.howItsDone: Some Hindu households and temples keep and care for cows and honor them as sacred. Vasishtha's Nandini belongs to the wondrous cows of Hindu story, cows said to give what is wished for.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shantanu and Ganga: seven sons given to the river, and the eighth spared when the king finally spoke. Where could you see only part of the story? Day seven hundred seven.

His wife has just told Shantanu she is Ganga, and that his seven lost sons were the Vasus, gods under a curse. His promise is broken, and she's about to go. So he asks the one thing he still can: what did the Vasus do, that they had to be born as men and die as babies? Ganga answers him before she leaves. Her answer starts on a mountainside, with a sage and his cow.
screen: `WHAT DID THEY DO?` → `GANGA ANSWERS BEFORE SHE GOES.` → `A SAGE AND HIS COW.`

segments.voice: The sage is Vasishtha. He keeps his hermitage on a mountain slope, and he owns a wondrous cow named Nandini. One day the Vasus come wandering there with their wives. One of the wives sees the cow and wants her, not for herself, but for a friend on earth, a princess, so that her friend might stay young and free of illness. Her husband is a Vasu named Dyu. He knows whose cow this is. But to please his wife, and with his brothers helping, he takes her. Vasishtha comes back to an empty pasture. He looks with a sage's inner sight, sees what happened, and curses the Vasus: they will be born on earth as men. The Vasus come and beg him to take it back. And here's the part to notice. Vasishtha can't unsay the curse. But he can shape what follows it. The seven who helped, he says, will be freed soon after they're born. Dyu, the one who took the cow, will live a long life on earth. And Vasishtha fills that life in: he'll be virtuous and learned, devoted to his father, and he'll have no children. So the eighth son, the one Shantanu saved by speaking, is Dyu, the thief himself. Then Ganga takes the child and goes. This whole week has turned on words that bind. A son's curse on a king. A young sage's single request. A sentence in Brahma's court. A vow by a river. And now a sage who can't take back his words, and spends his next ones making them bearable.
screen: `NANDINI, THE SAGE'S COW.` · `DYU TAKES HER TO PLEASE HIS WIFE.` · `THE CURSE: BORN AS MEN.` · `SEVEN FREED; DYU MUST LIVE.` · then, large: `WORDS HE COULDN'T UNSAY.`

segments.voice: Settle where you are, and let a few breaths go by without steering them. Bring to mind something you said that you can't take back: a sharp sentence, a no, a word in anger. It's said. Let it be said. Now, instead of replaying it, ask a different question: what could come after it? A softer word. An explanation. A small kindness to the person it landed on. Don't plan a speech. Just let one next word come to mind, and breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Shantanu and Ganga. A river goddess explaining, as she leaves, why the eighth son has to stay.
Your line: Shantanu and Ganga. Today, if you say something you can't take back, add a better word after it. Day seven hundred seven.

fork.setup: you're Vasishtha. the Vasus who stole your cow come begging you to lift your curse. what do you do?
options: lift it completely.
send them away unheard.
let it stand, but shape what follows.
fork.reveal: he can't unsay it, but he shapes it: seven freed soon after birth, and Dyu, who took the cow, to live a long, virtuous life with no children.

original.note: Sanskrit Nandinī, the name of Vasishtha's cow in this story.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Vasus were cursed for no reason the story gives.
what it means: one of them stole a sage's cow to please his wife, and his brothers helped.
what a scholar hears: Ganga tells Shantanu of Vasishtha's cow as she leaves, explaining why the eighth son must live long.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Ganga explains the Vasus' curse: Vasishtha's cow Nandini, Dyu's theft, the softened curse)
